'''Gabriel Andrew Dirac''' (13 March 1925 – 20 July 1984) was a Hungarian-British mathematician who mainly worked in [[graph theory]].<ref name=jgtobit>{{cite journal |last=Thomassen |first=Carsten |date=1985 |title=Gabriel Andrew Dirac Obituary |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1002/jgt.3190090302 |journal=Journal of Graph Theory |volume=9 |pages=303–318 |doi=10.1002/jgt.3190090302 |s2cid=28656582 |access-date=2021-05-01|url-access=subscription }}</ref> He served as [[Erasmus Smith's Professor of Mathematics]] at [[Trinity College Dublin]] from 1964 to 1966.<ref>{{cite book |last=Webb |first=D.A. |editor-first=Barlett |editor-last=J.R.|date=1992 |title=Trinity College Dublin Record Volume 1991 |location=Dublin |publisher=Trinity College Dublin Press |isbn=1-871408-07-5|page=}}</ref> In 1952, he gave a sufficient condition for a graph to contain a [[Hamiltonian circuit]]. The previous year, he conjectured that n points in the plane, not all collinear, must span at least <math>\lfloor n/2\rfloor</math> [[Sylvester–Gallai theorem|two-point line]]s, where <math>\lfloor x\rfloor</math> is the largest integer not exceeding <math>x</math>. This conjecture was proven for sufficiently large <math>n</math> by [[Ben Green (mathematician)|Green]] and [[Terence Tao|Tao]] in 2012.<ref>{{cite arXiv|last1=Green|first1=Ben|last2=Tao|first2=Terence|date=2012-08-23|title=On sets defining few ordinary lines|eprint=1208.4714|class=math.CO}}</ref>

==Education==
Dirac started his studies at [[St John's College, Cambridge]] in 1942, but in that same year, the war saw him serving in the aircraft industry.<ref name=jgtobit/> He received his MA in 1949, and moved to the [[University of London]], getting his Ph.D. "On the Colouring of Graphs: Combinatorial topology of Linear Complexes" there under [[Richard Rado]].<ref>{{MathGenealogy|id=42235}}</ref>

==Career==
Dirac's main academic positions were at the [[King's College London]] (1948-1954), [[University of Toronto]] (1952-1953), [[University of Vienna]] (1954-1958), [[University of Hamburg]] (1958-1963), [[Trinity College Dublin]] ([[Erasmus Smith's Professor of Mathematics]], 1964-1966), [[University of Wales at Swansea]] (1967-1970), and [[Aarhus University]] (1970-1984).<ref name=jgtobit/>

==Family==
He was born Balázs Gábor in [[Budapest]], to Richárd Balázs, a military officer and businessman, and Margit "Manci" Wigner (sister of [[Eugene Wigner]]).<ref>{{cite web | url=https://docplayer.hu/7508090-Magyar-tudomany-100-eve-szuletett-wigner-jeno-400-eve-szuletett-otto-von-guericke.html | title=Magyar Tudomány. 100 ÉVE SZÜLETETT WIGNER JENÕ 400 ÉVE SZÜLETETT OTTO von GUERICKE | publisher=DocPlayer | language=hu | accessdate=29 January 2022}}</ref> When his mother married [[Paul Dirac]] in 1937, he and his sister resettled in England and were formally adopted, changing their family name to Dirac.<ref>{{MacTutor|id=Dirac|title=Paul Adrien Maurice Dirac}}</ref> He married Rosemari Paulsen and they had four children together.<ref>{{cite book | url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0167506008704448 | title=Gabriel Andrew Dirac. | series=Annals of Discrete Mathematics | year=1988 | volume=41 | pages=1–6 | publisher=Elsevier | doi=10.1016/S0167-5060(08)70444-8 | isbn=9780444871299 | language=en | accessdate=16 December 2022}}</ref>
